title: The distribution that does not move

prereqs.why: The equation pi P = pi is what has to be solved, and the normalising condition is what makes the answer unique.
That a distribution multiplies the matrix on the left is what makes the equation a column-by-column one.

statement:
A Markov chain on $\{1,2,3\}$ has transition matrix

$$P = \begin{pmatrix}
\tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0\\[2pt]
\tfrac13 & \tfrac13 & \tfrac13\\[2pt]
0 & \tfrac14 & \tfrac34
\end{pmatrix}.$$

It is irreducible and aperiodic, so it has a unique stationary distribution
$\pi = (\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3)$ — the unique row vector with non-negative
entries summing to $1$ that satisfies $\pi P = \pi$.

Give $\pi_3$ exactly.
hints: $\pi P = \pi$ means $\sum_i \pi_i p_{i,j} = \pi_j$ for each $j$ — a sum down **column** $j$ of $P$, not along a row.
Write the three equations out. The one for $j = 1$ involves only $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$, so start there.
Column 1 gives $\pi_1 = \tfrac12\pi_1 + \tfrac13\pi_2$, so $\pi_2 = \tfrac32 \pi_1$. Column 3 then gives $\pi_3$ in terms of $\pi_1$ too.
One of the three equations is redundant — it always is. Use two of them plus $\pi_1 + \pi_2 + \pi_3 = 1$.

payload.label: $\pi_3 =$
payload.syntax: A number or a fraction. Arithmetic is fine.
